[0] everyday_reading (E): In maths, = states a symmetric, lasting equality (a = b means b = a, and x = x + 5 is false). In Java, = is a one-time, directed action: evaluate the right side, then store the result in the variable on the left.
[1] misconception (M) -> VariablesHoldExpressions: wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
[2] misconception (M) -> AssignCompares: wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
[3] misconception (M) -> AssignmentNotExpression: wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
[4] misconception (M) -> AssignmentOppositeDirection: wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
[5] misconception (M) -> AssignmentAddsToTarget: wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.
[6] misconception (M) -> AssignmentIsEquation: wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
[7] misconception (M) -> AssignmentExchangesValues: wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
[8] misconception (M) -> AssignmentEmptiesSource: wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.
[9] inconsistent_trace (T) -> VariablesHoldExpressions: Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
[10] misconception (M) -> SwapWithoutTemp: wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
[11] misconception (M) -> AssignmentCopiesObject: wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
[12] misconception (M) -> VariableKeepsOldValue: wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

[0] names_the_element (N): Assignment statement: the statement variable = expression; which stores a data-type value in a variable.
[1] states_the_rule (S): The left-hand side must be a single variable. The right-hand side can be any expression whose type is compatible with the variable's type. = is not mathematical equality (a + b = b + a and 1 = a are illegal).

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): First the right-hand side is fully evaluated using the variables' current values (left to right). Then that value is stored in the left-hand variable, replacing its old value, and execution moves to the next statement.
[1] output_prediction (OP): As a statement it prints nothing; its result is the new value of the left variable (after c = a + b; with a = 1234 and b = 99, c is 1333). Used as an expression, its value is the value assigned.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Exactly one variable, the left one, changes, and its old value is lost. Variables on the right keep their values: x = x + 5; with x = 5 makes x 10.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The left side must be a declared variable whose type accepts the value. Assignment is how that variable's value changes.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A declaration can include the first assignment (int x = 5;). Assigning to a variable that was never declared does not compile.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Exchanging a[i] and a[j] takes three assignments in a fixed order through a temporary, because each assignment overwrites its target.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): int t = a; a = b; b = t; works only in this order, because every assignment destroys its left variable's old value.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): x op= e is shorthand for x = x op e. The left variable's current value is fetched first and then combined with e.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): Because an assignment is an expression whose value is the value stored, and = groups right to left, a = b = 0 first stores 0 in b and then stores that 0 in a.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): As a statement, i++ has the same effect as the assignment i = i + 1.
[7] relation_to_neighbour (R): A trace records the value of each variable after each assignment runs, one row per statement.
[8] relation_to_neighbour (R): x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
[9] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Assignment gives a variable its value in each role: initialization, counter update (n = n + 1), gatherer update (sum = sum + x), most-wanted holder update (max = x), or temporary (t = a).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> VariablesHoldExpressions: Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The left-hand side of = must be a single variable; only the right-hand side may be an arbitrary expression. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Any assignment whose left side is a literal or compound expression (7 = a; a + b = c;): 'unexpected type, required: variable'.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use assignment whenever a variable's value must be set or updated. Use == to compare, final to forbid updates, and op= or ++ for x = x op e.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A local variable may be declared only once in its scope; later changes use an assignment without the type. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: A second 'int x = ...' for a name already declared in the same or an enclosing block: 'variable x is already defined'.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A final variable is assigned exactly once; it cannot be reassigned after initialization. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Any assignment, ++ or op= to a final variable after its initialization: 'cannot assign a value to final variable'.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: = assigns and == compares; a condition needs a boolean. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing if (a = b) with int a, b gives 'incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean'. With boolean variables it compiles and silently assigns.
[6] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The assigned value's type must fit the variable's type. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Assigning a double to an int, an int to a String, and so on: 'incompatible types'.
